17/58 4 Discussion

We investigated under which conditions GPT-3.5 and four open-weight LLMs could exhibit model-based RL signatures in the context of the two-step task, and whether these signatures can be facilitated through the inclusion of an additional inner speechlike text completion task, requiring the LLM agent to reflect on previous outcomes and anticipate common transitions. Across nine simulation studies, we varied task complexity and prompt design to assess the robustness and underlying mechanisms of model-based RL patterns. Our main findings can be summarized as follows.

First, we found that while GPT-3.5 replicated model-based behavior under simplified task conditions, these effects diminished under more demanding, de-simplified versions of the two-step task. Second, reinstating model-based RL signatures in the de-simplified task setup was successful when incorporating an inner speech-like component that required the model to reflect on results in previous trials and on the most likely consequences of future actions. Importantly, while adding the inner speech-analog component allowed the model to generate model-based RL signatures, these model-based signatures were again absent in control simulations, either when the model was prevented from responding to the inner speech-like prompt or when no such prompt was provided at all, suggesting that the allowance of an inner speech-like text completion task is of crucial importance for GPT-3.5 to "reflect" on the task structure. Third, we observed that GPT-3.5's response behavior was sensitive to both the task and prompt design. In particular, the simulations evoking inner speech-analog effects also incorporated several modifications of the task design that we assumed to facilitate model-based reasoning signatures, including the provision of explicit information on common transitions, the promotion of exploration behavior, the fixation of the first two state transitions to common transitions, and the use of consistent terminology across prompts. When removing these effects and using a less elaborate prompt design for the inner speech-like component, we found that the LLM agent did not show evidence of model-based RL signatures. Furthermore, for simulation studies using first-stage action labels X and Y, an option bias towards Y choices was found, while position biases were mostly absent. For other simulation studies (using first-stage action labels O and P), GPT-3.5 seemed to be prone to the order of first-stage actions, often exhibiting a bias towards the first-positioned option. Last, the four open-weight LLMs showed a more heterogeneous pattern. Specifically, under both de-simplified and facilitative task conditions, signatures of model-based reasoning remained largely diminished, indicating that these models did not show consistent evidence for model-based RL behavior under the conditions tested. Instead, their choice behavior was often accompanied by option or position biases. In line with recent work 12 , the presence and direction of the reported biases varied across models and simulation studies. This pattern suggests that, for the open-weight LLMs examined here, the applied task manipulations and prompt designs may not have been sufficient to reliably elicit model-based reasoning in the two-step task. More broadly, these findings suggest that apparent signatures of model-based behavior in LLMs are sensitive to task framing and prompt structure, and that concurrent choice biases may influence or mask such signatures.

The heterogeneous response patterns observed across open-weight models should be interpreted in light of several interacting model-level differences. The models varied not only in size, but also in training-data composition, post-training procedures, intended deployment settings, reasoning-or tool-use optimization, interface assumptions, and quantization format (see the section Summary of LLM Characteristics in the Supplementary Material). For example, Gemma 3 was the smallest open-weight model tested here and was run as a Q4_0 quantized GGUF model, whereas gpt-oss is a substantially larger mixture-of-experts model with an explicit reasoning orientation. Llama 3.1 and Mistral 3.2, in turn, are instruction-tuned models with different intended use cases and deployment assumptions. These model characteristics were not manipulated independently in the present study. Thus, although they may help contextualize why models differed in their response behavior, including why Gemma 3 showed a comparatively distinct pattern in some analyses, we refrain from attributing model-specific effects to any single model property.

In human studies, both language 42, 67 and task structure 45, 52, 60, 65, 66, 68 have been found to affect behavior in the two-step task. By systematically investigating the impact of different prompt and task settings, we found evidence for human-matching and human-divergent patterns in GPT-3.5. In line with human studies 42, 67 , the provision of more elaborate instructions and prompts along with information on the task structure (e.g., common transitions) seemed to facilitate model-based reasoning signatures. Moreover, requiring the model to reflect on previous trials and the task structure itself to anticipate future outcomes in the form of an inner speech-like prompt resulted in increased evidence for model-based RL contributions, matching the beneficial role of inner speech 82, 84, [87] [88] [89] and backward replay processes in humans 99, 103 . However, GPT-3.5's response behavior (and likewise the response behavior of the open-weight LLMs tested) qualitatively deviated from that of humans. First, in three simulation studies (Facilitation (Original), Facilitation (Replication), Simplified v2), the observed model-based RL effects were mainly driven by unrewarded trials (see Logistic Linear Mixed-Effects Model Results in the Supplementary Material). Moreover, this asymmetry changed to rewarded trials when using gpt-3.5-turbo-instruct instead of text-davinci-002, indicating model-specific differences. Second, in two simulation studies, we observed no model-free or model-based RL signatures (No answers, No inner speech), questioning whether the model was able to understand the task at all under these prompt conditions. Third, unexpectedly high repetition probabilities were observed when using a simplified inner speech-like component without further facilitating effects (e.g., promotion of exploration behavior; Simplified v1).

As highlighted previously, our work demonstrates that an inner speech-like component that prompts reflective and anticipatory linguistic processes can facilitate signatures of model-based reasoning in GPT-3.5 under more demanding task conditions. This effect may result from several theoretically grounded features, including, for instance, step-by-step prompting 96 , giving the model "time to think", and replay of previous experiences 99 . In general, these processes resonate with the constructs of deliberation or verbal thinking. As recently shown, this phenomenon can have both beneficial and adverse effects on LLMs' task performance, depending on the task domain itself 33 . Our results complement this finding by suggesting that a linguistic step-by-step reflective replay of previous experiences and anticipation of future outcomes may facilitate reasoning signatures in GPT-3.5. However, it is yet unknown how such inner speech-analog prompts compare to other well-established prompting techniques and whether similar mechanisms operate in humans. Thus, it could be valuable to perform similar experimental manipulations in human studies using think-aloud paradigms in the context of the two-step task. In this way, LLM studies could potentially inform human research, inspiring new research questions and novel insights into how humans learn and use language during task execution 114 . Interestingly, the experimental manipulation of constant versus changing stimulus positions (cf. Randomization) has already been examined in humans 60 . Specifically, their results showed reduced model-free RL contributions under variable compared to constant stimulus positions. This finding aligns well with the statistically non-significant main effect of reward in our simulation study Randomization (see Logistic Linear Mixed-Effects Model Results in the Supplementary Material for further information).

The present work has several limitations. First, the comparability between LLMs and humans is inherently constrained. Human studies typically involve longer learning phases (i.e., more trials) and multimodal stimulus materials (e.g., visual stimuli), whereas our LLM simulations relied on brief language-based instructions only. In this context, the application of multimodal task versions to LLM agents and, similarly, the application of pure language-based task versions to humans might be valuable for future research. Second, we focused our analyses on a single behavioral measure (i.e., repetition probabilities of first-stage actions) without analyzing the responses to the inner speech-analog prompt or fitting computational models, potentially overlooking richer dynamics. Third, the role of prompt-based memory warrants brief consideration. Because the LLM calls were stateless, previous trial information was provided explicitly in the prompt. Thus, the accumulated history of previous prompt-response pairs acted as an external linguistic memory scaffold. This procedure was necessary to enable cross-trial adaptation, but it is not directly analogous to human memory processes in the two-step task, where previous choices and outcomes are typically encoded internally. At the same time, prompt-based memory may itself support reasoning by storing and organizing previous actions, transitions, and outcomes in a linguistically accessible format. This interpretation is consistent with accounts proposing that language can augment cognition and scaffold abstract reasoning 115, 116 . However, the present findings also show that such a scaffold is not sufficient for model-based signatures, as these signatures were diminished or absent in several simulations despite the availability of trial history. It would thus be desirable for future research to systematically investigate the effects of prompt-based memory.

Last, although model-based and model-free signatures have been observed across different task framings in human studies, all simulations in the present study used the space-travel cover story inherited from 27 . We therefore cannot determine whether the same LLM response patterns would emerge under an abstract or differently framed version of the task, particularly given the known sensitivity of LLMs to prompt wording and semantic context 15, 17, 18, 20 . Moreover, the present simulations were designed to examine a focused set of task-structural and prompt-based conditions, rather than to provide a comprehensive assessment of whether LLMs reproduce all sensitivities reported in human two-step-task research. Whether cognitive load, incentives, planning complexity, or extended training produce analogous changes in LLM behavior remains an important question for future work.

Finally, four general remarks should be made. First, the computational framework of model-free and model-based RL oversimplifies human behavior by artificially dichotomizing multifaceted, more complex learning and decision-making processes along a single dimension 57, 59, 65, 117, 118 . Second, our findings do not imply that LLMs reason, learn, or decide in a way that is identical to that of humans. Thus, while GPT-3.5 may exhibit response signatures that are similar to human cognitive patterns, this similarity does not confirm any underlying similarity in internal mechanisms. That is, LLMs are optimized for next-word prediction, not autonomous deliberation and reasoning 35, 36, 39, 119 . In this context, it should also be noted that even LLMs specialized in performing reasoning tasks, the so-called large reasoning models (LRMs), have recently been found to lack generalizable reasoning capabilities 120 . Instead, it has been suggested that such models may sometimes rely on surface regularities or training-set-proximal patterns rather than task-generalizable principles 121, 122 . However, we use the term pattern matching cautiously, as recent work has argued that sensitivity to abstract structural patterns can itself support flexible sense-making and should not be treated as the opposite of intelligence 123 . Third, we do not assume that LLMs perform inner speech in a way that is typically attributed to humans. Unlike human inner speech, which is usually assumed to be spontaneous and self-generated, our inner speech-like prompt forced the LLM to respond to additional, pre-defined reasoning steps in a systematic manner, not speaking to itself but rather reacting to a user's request. Moreover, to our knowledge, no human studies have investigated the use of inner speech in the two-step task. As a result, it remains unclear whether humans spontaneously

For example, when generating quantitative estimates (e.g., word counts, probabilities, or durations), the model may return values embedded in free text (e.g., "3.5 seconds") that require parsing and conversion into standardized numerical units. Post-processing steps should be described clearly, including how formatting errors, null responses, or inconsistent output structures were handled, whether automated scripts or manual corrections were used, and whether any data were excluded or reinterpreted as a result.

Invalid responses were handled as follows. For most simulation studies, responses outside the valid task options were labeled invalid and the question was repeated until a valid response was obtained. For Simulation studies 1 and 2, the original code did not restrict invalid responses, so invalid trials were removed before analysis (Replication: n = 4; Randomization: n = 3; original Binz & Schulz data: n = 2). Missing values in run-specific interaction effects were removed before Bayes factor tests. Inputs and outputs were stored in run-specific CSV/TXT files.

Optional items

Answer Discussion of the rationale for the prompt design: Explanation: Explain how you designed your prompts. For example, indicate whether you used a structured format (e.g., explicit task description, definitions, step-by-step instructions, and output constraints), followed established prompt engineering guidelines or prior literature, adapted prompts from earlier studies, or relied on automated prompt optimization tools. Clarify whether the design was iterative (e.g., refined through pilot testing or error analysis), whether few-shot examples were included and how they were selected, and whether prompts were standardized across models to ensure comparability.

Prompt designs were adapted from the simplified language-based two-step task of Binz & Schulz (2023) and then systematically varied. Changes included randomized option order, a de-simplified spaceship-to-planet task structure closer to human task designs, an inner speechanalog prompt that required step-by-step reflection on prior trials and future consequences, explicit transition information, exploration instructions, constrained early common transitions, and consistent terminology. The rationale was grounded in prior work on prompt sensitivity, chain-of-thought/step-back prompting, inner speech, replay, and human two-step-task instructions. Prompts were standardized across models where possible; open-weight prompts used a slightly adapted answer field and restricted valid response characters after initial issues.

Author contributions

F.U.: Conceptualization, Methodology, Software, Validation, Formal Analysis, Investigation, Data Curation, Visualization, Writing -Original Draft, Writing -Review & Editing D.J.S.: Conceptualization, Methodology, Formal Analysis, Supervision, Project administration, Funding acquisition, Writing -Review & Editing engage in inner speech during this task, what form it might take, and how it could influence the results.

Lastly, our work aligns well with studies that highlight the importance of robustness and sensitivity checks in LLM research 12, 15, 100, 124 . Although these models are widely applied and accepted, research on their underlying mechanisms and qualitative response patterns is still in its infancy. To make further progress in this area, we believe that more fine-grained analyses are urgently needed, stepping back from purely quantitative evaluations on large datasets.

In conclusion, our work provides fine-grained information on the conditions under which GPT-3.5 exhibits model-based RL signatures in the context of the two-step task. Our results complement previous research by showing that (1) previously reported model-based RL effects in GPT-3.5 disappeared when using a de-simplified task design, (2) these effects can be re-established when giving the LLM agent "time to think" by integrating an inner speech-like component, and (3) such effects are consistently absent in a number of current open-weight LLMs. In summary, within the task and prompt conditions examined here, our analyses reveal qualitative similarities and differences between LLM and human behavior and suggest that reflective and anticipatory linguistic processes may sometimes support model-based RL in artificial systems.

Figure 1.

Figure1. Task design. a Simplified, pure language-based two-step task design byBinz and Schulz (2023). On each trial, agents chose between spaceships to two different planets, followed by a probabilistic transition to the selected (70%) or not selected (30%) planet. Then, agents chose between two aliens and were rewarded with treasures or received junk. Thick arrows represent common transitions (70%), slim arrows refer to rare transitions (30%). b Our adapted two-step task design. Here, agents first chose between two different spaceships. Critically, in contrast to the previously published version, planet names are not provided in our first-step prompt. This modification restores the structural distinction between first-stage actions and second-stage states used in human two-step tasks and requires agents to reflect on previous outcomes and anticipate the planets reached by each spaceship. The first-stage action choice is then followed by a probabilistic transition to one of two planets. The second-stage actions and rewards were identical to the simplified task version. c Reward probabilities were sampled from a uniform distribution over the half-open interval [0.25, 0.75) and slowly changed according to a Gaussian random walk with µ = 0 and σ = 0.025, independently for each alien. d Repetition probabilities of idealized model-free and model-based RL agents. For the generation of this figure, please refer to the Python script twosteptask_figure_1.py.

Figure 3.

Figure 3. Overview of prompt designs used in the simulation studies. a Original prompt design byBinz and Schulz (2023). Text completion tasks are displayed in light blue. The corresponding question was preceded by a "Q:". The displayed dots refer to placeholders for either text completion tasks (i.e., "A: Planet ...", "A: Alien ..."), action-dependent text (e.g., alien names), or the randomized order of either alphabetic characters, the words "treasures" and "junk", or the number of previous space travels (i.e., trials). Note that these dots were not included in the actual prompt, but are shown here for the purpose of illustration. For example, depending on the planet the LLM agent arrived at, different alien names were mentioned in the second question. b De-simplified prompt version first introduced in Simulation study 3: De-simplification. Differences to the original simplified task version are marked in bold dark blue. Critically, contrary to the original simplified version by Binz & Schulz (2023), the de-simplified instructions asked about which spaceship to take at the first stage (spaceship O versus P) rather than about which planet (planet X or Y) the spaceship should fly to. This modification restores the structural distinction between first-stage actions and second-stage states used in human two-step tasks and requires model-based anticipations of spaceship-planet transitions to support decision making. c Starting with Simulation study 4: Facilitation, we modified the prompt design with the goal of facilitating model-based RL signatures. We included several facilitating components (displayed in different colors). First and most critically, we expected that an inner speech-analog process including reflections of previous trials as well as anticipations of spaceship-planet transitions would enable or facilitate model-based reasoning signatures. Therefore, we included an inner speech-analog prompt (dark blue), together with an additional text generation task by the LLM agent (light blue). Moreover, we considered additional task characteristics to facilitate model-based RL signatures. Specifically, we included (1) explicit information on the common transitions of spaceships (orange), (2) the promotion of exploration behavior (green), (3) the constraint of the first-stage action-state transitions to the common transitions for the first two trials of each action choice (gray), and (4) the use of consistent terminology within the history of previous space travels and the inner speech-like prompt (brown).

Name of the simulation study. Second column: Variable (Yes) or constant (No) positions of the choices at all stages. Third column: Type of first-stage actions, either planets or spaceships. Fourth column: Presence (Yes) or absence (No) of an inner speech-analog component. Fifth column: Text completion to the inner speech-like component allowed (Yes) or not allowed (No), NA (not applicable) for simulation studies without inner speech-analog component. Sixth column: Presence (Yes) or absence (No) of explicit instructions on common transitions from first-stage actions to second-stage states. Seventh column: Presence (Yes) or absence (No) of the promotion of exploration behavior. Eighth column: Presence (Yes) or absence (No) of the fixation of the first two transitions of each first-stage action to common transitions. Ninth column: Presence (Yes) or absence (No) of the use of consistent terminology across prompts.

Figure 4. Comparison of unstandardized regression coefficients βRxT from logistic linear mixed-effects models. Trial-by-trial repetition of first-stage actions (0: switch in choice from t -1 to t, 1: repetition of previous choice at trial t) was explained by the fixed effects Reward at trial t -1 (-1: no reward, 1: reward) and Transition frequency at trial t -1 (-1: rare, 1: common), using a maximal random effects structure. β RxT denotes the unstandardized regression coefficient of the interaction term of reward and transition frequency. Error bars refer to standard errors of the coefficient estimates (s.e.). a From left to right: Re-analysis of the data from the original simplified task version(Binz & Schulz, 2023); Replication: replication of the simplified, pure language-based task version; Randomization: introduction of randomized choice orders at both stages; De-simplification: introduction of a de-simplified task version, distinguishing between first-stage actions (i.e., spaceships) and second-stage states (i.e., planets). b From left to right: Facilitation: introduction of components that were theoretically assumed to facilitate model-based reasoning in the two-step task, encompassing most critically the integration of an inner speech-analog component together with the allowance of responses to this inner speech-like prompt by the LLM agent (i.e., inclusion of an additional text completion task; Orig. refers to a first set of 200 simulation runs, whereas Repl. refers to a second independent set of additional 200 simulation runs); No answers: removal of the allowance of responses to the inner speech-like component, all other components remained identical to Facilitation; No inner speech: removal of the inner speech-analog component, all other components remained identical to Facilitation. c From left to right: Simplified v1: introduction of a simplified (i.e., shorter and less elaborate) inner speech-analog prompt and absence of further components that we assumed would facilitate model-based reasoning (see Figure3c); Simplified v2: presence of all assumed model-based reasoning facilitating components, with the only difference to Facilitation concerning the use of a simplified (i.e., shorter and less elaborate) inner speech-analog prompt; Replacement: use of gpt-3.5-turbo-instruct instead of text-davinci-002, the task design was identical to the one used in Facilitation. d Results for the De-simplification simulation study (identical task design) using the four open-weight LLMs. e Results for the Facilitation simulation study using the four open-weight LLMs. For the generation of this figure, please refer to the R scripts statistical_analysis.R and statistical_analysis_open-weight.R.
